rv.q: Exactly how it ended up making its stage debut 32 years later at an off-West End theatre in Islington I am fairly unclear.

Edgar Hoover, who was Director of the FBI for almost 50 years. at King’s Head Theatre This comedy musical is a hilarious and clever clapback, throwing a parodic light onto the concealed sexualities, love affairs and parties of a man outwardly known for his machismo and active homophobia.

This is a gleefully satirical portrait of a tyrant who destroyed countless lives while concealing his own truth. More importantly, it’s a terrific musical. The book is razor-sharp, the lyrics sparkle with wit and Matz’s score effortlessly shifts from heartfelt ballads to vaudeville and classic musical theatre.

A high-camp comedy musical about this sinister figure’s life, then, may seem like a tall order. begins with Edgar (Mad Men’s Bryan Batt, amping up the repressed melancholy) on his deathbed, in a variant of It’s A Wonderful Life, with a younger version of himself guiding him back through his past choices.

Peter Matz’s music gives Shearer and Leopold’s witty lyrics an extra lift, and Bill Deamer’s choreography is worthy of Hollywood it its very best. It’s wonderful to see it at a small, intimate 200 seat live theatre in Islington. Everyone needs publicity, radio commentator Walter Winchell tells Hoover.

A secret homosexual himself, Hoover (played by Mad Men‘s Bryan Batt) maintained a lifestyle out of the public eye with his ‘lifetime assistant’ Clyde Tolson (1900-1975). Tolson (played by Hugo Bolton) is a figure who has appeared in many films about Hoover, and their relationship now seems accepted as fact.

With such great minds behind the project of course the show is satirical, but never in a pompous, self-important way. The satire instead feels more akin to Aristophanes’ treatment of his ancient Athenian contemporaries in his comedies. We lean into the ridiculous, to brilliant effect.

Edgar Hoover, the controversial, deeply flawed, and arguably villainous architect of the modern FBI, might not seem like the most obvious fodder for a musical. Yet, a new musical production attempts to do just that in Here Comes J.
While it is undoubtedly an enjoyable romp, it feels like the decades of development have left it in some kind of “Frankenstein’s monster” state, where elements feel disjointed.
